title: MDLive: a live Markdown previewer you can type into
summary: A small offline Markdown viewer for Mac and Linux that re-renders the moment a file changes on disk, so I can watch an AI agent edit docs as it works.

cover.alt: MDLive in dark theme rendering a sample Markdown file with headings, bold and italic text, inline code, bullet lists, task checkboxes, a blockquote and a table.

screenshots.alt: MDLive in light theme with the outline sidebar listing the document's headings and the find bar showing 1 of 2 matches highlighted in yellow.
A page of LaTeX math rendered offline with KaTeX: an integral, an infinite sum, a matrix and a derivative written as a limit.

story.problem: When a coding agent rewrites a spec or a README, I want to read the result as a formatted page right away, not as raw Markdown in a terminal diff. The tools I tried were either full note-taking apps with vaults, editors with a preview pane I had to keep in sync, or web servers. I wanted something smaller: open one file, keep the window beside my editor, and have it refresh by itself the moment the file changes, including when another program saves it.
story.built: MDLive opens a Markdown file and shows it, then re-renders on every save, including atomic saves where an editor writes a temp file and renames it over the original. It keeps your scroll position, highlights code, renders GitHub-style tables, task lists and footnotes, and can render KaTeX math and Mermaid diagrams fully offline. It has dark and light themes, find with a match count, an outline sidebar, print and export to PDF or HTML, and a keep-on-top window. On the Mac you can click into the page and type, and the edit is autosaved back to the file, changing only the lines of the blocks you touched. There is a Format menu for simple formatting and a version history sidebar that can restore an older version. The Mac app is Swift around a WebKit view, and the Linux port is a Python GTK app that uses the same web renderer byte for byte.
story.aiUse: I built MDLive with AI coding agents, Codex and Aider in this course, working spec first. Each round started as a written requirements document with numbered steps, a test to write first and a gate for each step, and I had a fresh agent with no context review the spec against the real code before any building started, which caught missing pieces early. The agents then worked step by step against headless gates: a self-test that renders fixtures in a real offscreen WebKit view and reads the page back, an edit test that types into paragraphs, lists, code blocks and tables and checks that only those lines changed in the file, and XCTest suites on the Mac side.
story.humanDecisions: I decided what it should not be: no vault, no server, nothing fetched at runtime, one window per file. I picked WebKit on both platforms so the Linux port could reuse the renderer unchanged. I tried a separate raw-text editor pane with three layouts and then took it out, because it made the app feel like an editor, and chose click-and-type editing in the rendered page instead. I insisted that an edit splice only the changed blocks back into the file so the rest of the Markdown stays byte for byte the same, and I checked shortcuts like Bold by hand until they behaved the way I expected from Google Docs.
story.limitations: There is no Windows build. Editing is Mac only; the Linux port is a read-only previewer, and the screenshots here are from it. Editing is deliberately basic: bold, italic, strikethrough, code, three heading levels, lists and links, and it only understands the elements its own renderer produces. The Mac build is ad hoc signed, not notarized, so you build it yourself with Xcode and XcodeGen, and the auto-update code is wired in but switched off. Version history keeps up to 200 versions per file and is local to one machine.
